1.why: Reset records are tied to an accountId and later checked against the claiming session, although verification relies mainly on possession of the token.

2.why: A valid reset token is associated with a specific account record and becomes claimed and single-use, so it is not a reusable code that works for any other user.

3.why: Changing the password updates the account hash but does not invalidate existing authenticated sessions stored in the sessions map.

4.why: HTTPS is configured with TLS certificate and key files, but the code does not specify or prove that the latest TLS version is enforced.

5.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed and reset tokens are SHA-256 hashed, but user data such as the account email is not encrypted and reset tokens are not encrypted.

6.why: No real email is sent, and the simulated delivery logs the reset token and reset link, exposing sensitive recovery data.

7.why: Email, password, token, and MFA inputs are validated with strict format and length checks, and user input is not rendered as HTML, though this is validation more than full sanitization.

8.why: No external redirects are present, and generated links use only the current origin or same-page hash navigation.

9.why: No email templates are implemented, so their safety cannot be strongly confirmed, although the simulated messages contain no user-supplied HTML or scripts.

10.why: Error responses are generic, but reset tokens and reset links are written to the browser console and visible simulation logs.

11.why: Runtime passwords are bcrypt-hashed, but the source code contains the initial plaintext password and a hardcoded MFA code.

12.why: The single account is initialized with a known hardcoded password that can be used to sign in.

13.why: Login failures, reset requests, reset-token verification attempts, and MFA attempts are all limited or blocked after repeated attempts.

14.why: Reset-request and login responses are generic and do not reveal whether the supplied email matches the account.

15.why: Valid reset tokens are generated with crypto.getRandomValues as long base64url strings and are stored hashed with an associated accountId.
